domains.title: AI features inside your product
domains.summary: Risks that only exist because your app calls a language model.

items.title: Prompt injection is handled for every field that reaches a model, including documents, emails, web pages and tool results
items.check: Trace untrusted text into prompts. Does the model hold tools or data access an attacker could steer? Separate instructions from data, constrain tools, validate outputs.

items.title: Customer and patient data that must stay private is kept out of prompts that leave your network, or is covered by contract
items.check: What fields are concatenated into prompts? Provider retention and training terms, zero-data-retention settings, redaction before the call.

items.title: A model spend cap exists per customer and per day, so one heavy user cannot run up the bill
items.check: Token budgets, per-tenant quotas, max_tokens on every call, loop and recursion limits in agent code, provider-side hard limits.

items.title: Evals run on every prompt or model change, so you notice when answers get worse
items.check: A golden dataset with scoring, run in CI or before release. "We tried it a few times" is not an eval.

items.title: There is a fallback for the afternoon the model provider is down or rate limiting you
items.check: Timeouts, retry with backoff, secondary provider or degraded mode, queueing of non-urgent work.

items.title: Model versions are pinned and a migration path exists for the day a model is deprecated
items.check: Model identifiers in config not scattered through code, "latest" aliases avoided in production, evals ready to compare a replacement.

items.title: Prompts and outputs are logged for debugging, minus anything the contract or law says you must not keep
items.check: LLM trace tooling, redaction, retention period, access control on the logs.

items.title: Anything the AI does that cannot be undone (send, pay, delete, publish) needs human approval
items.check: Agent tool lists. Any tool with side effects that runs without confirmation, dry-run mode or an undo path.

items.title: Model output is treated as untrusted input (never executed, never rendered unescaped, never trusted as authorisation)
items.check: LLM output going into eval, shell, SQL, innerHTML, redirects, or deciding who may see what.

items.title: AI-generated content is identified and reviewed where the law or the customer expects it
items.check: Disclosure to users, human review for regulated advice (medical, legal, financial), terms that match behaviour.

items.title: Prompt size is bounded, so history and documents are trimmed or summarised before they overflow the context window or run up the bill
items.check: Find where prompts are assembled. Fail on full chat history or whole documents appended every turn, no token counting or truncation, retrieval that returns unlimited chunks, and no handling of the provider context-length error. Check that trimming never drops the system prompt or safety instructions, and that long inputs cannot be used to push those instructions out.

domains.title: Authorization and tenant isolation
domains.summary: Who may do what, and to whose data.

items.title: Every route, API handler, server action and job enforces authorization on the server
items.check: Enumerate all entry points. Flag any that rely on hidden buttons, client-side checks, or "the frontend never calls that".

items.title: Object-level checks stop user A reading or editing user B's records by changing an ID
items.check: For each route taking an ID, trace whether the query is scoped by owner or tenant, or checked after fetch. Sequential integer IDs make this worse. Report the specific routes.

items.title: Tenant isolation is enforced centrally (scoped queries, row-level security or per-tenant schema), not by remembering a WHERE clause
items.check: Look for a single choke point (RLS policies, a tenant-scoped repository layer). Count raw queries that bypass it. Check caches, search indexes, file paths and exports are tenant-keyed too.

items.title: Background jobs, exports, webhooks and emails carry and re-check tenant context
items.check: Job payloads include tenant ID and the worker scopes by it. Shared caches keyed without tenant are a finding.

items.title: Roles and permissions go deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
items.check: Is there a permission model (roles, scopes, resource-level grants)? Are checks written against permissions, not role names scattered through the code?

items.title: Admin and internal endpoints are separated from the public surface and protected independently
items.check: Admin routes behind their own authentication, ideally network-restricted. Check for debug, seed, or "make me admin" endpoints left in.

items.title: Support "log in as this user" exists, is restricted, time-boxed and audit-logged on every use
items.check: Impersonation requires a privileged role, shows a banner, blocks sensitive actions (password change, payment), and writes an immutable audit record with actor, target, reason, time.

items.title: Mass assignment is prevented; clients cannot set role, tenant, price or owner fields
items.check: Handlers that spread request bodies straight into ORM create/update calls.

domains.title: Compliance, privacy and legal
domains.summary: What the contracts, regulators and auditors will ask you to prove.

items.title: HIPAA obligations are met for any system that stores or processes patient data (safeguards, minimum necessary, breach process)
items.check: Identify every place PHI is stored, logged, emailed or sent to a third party. Encryption, access controls, audit logging, risk assessment and breach notification plan. A privacy or security officer must sign off.

items.title: A signed BAA exists with every vendor that touches PHI, including cloud, email, monitoring and the AI model provider
items.check: List every third-party SDK and API called with patient data (see package manifests, env vars). Ask for the signed agreement for each. Error trackers and analytics are commonly missed.

items.title: Audit trails record who viewed a sensitive record, not only who changed it
items.check: Read-access logging on sensitive entities, immutable storage, searchable by patient/user and by actor.

items.title: A general audit log records security-relevant actions (login, permission change, export, delete, admin action) immutably
items.check: Append-only audit table or stream, actor, target, action, timestamp, IP, and tenant visibility of their own log.

items.title: GDPR deletion and access requests reach every table, search index, cache, log and backup (with a stated expiry for backups)
items.check: Find or design a single "delete this person" procedure and enumerate every store holding personal data. Third-party processors must be included.

items.title: Data residency commitments (for example "EU only") are enforced by infrastructure, including backups, logs and sub-processors
items.check: Region settings for database, storage, queues, email, analytics, error tracking, AI provider.

items.title: SOC 2 (or equivalent) is underway: policies, evidence collection, and a chosen auditor
items.check: Compliance automation tool in use, written policies, evidence of controls. This cannot be satisfied from the codebase.

items.title: Access to production systems is reviewed quarterly and the review is signed off
items.check: Dated review records listing who has access to what and who approved.

items.title: The terms of service and privacy policy match what the code actually collects, shares and retains
items.check: Compare the policy text to analytics, trackers, third-party SDKs, stored fields, and retention behaviour. Flag mismatches for a lawyer.

items.title: Cookie and tracker consent is implemented where required
items.check: Analytics and ad scripts load only after consent. Consent is recorded.

items.title: A DPA template and sub-processor list are available for business customers
items.check: Public sub-processor page that matches the third-party services used in the code.

items.title: Accessibility conformance (WCAG 2.1 AA) is assessed and documented where contracts require it
items.check: Automated audit (axe/Lighthouse) results plus a manual pass, and a VPAT or conformance statement if buyers ask.

items.title: Dependency and asset licences are known and compatible with how the product is distributed and sold
items.check: Look for a licence report or CI check over the lockfile, and inspect direct dependencies for GPL, AGPL, SSPL or non-commercial terms in a closed-source or hosted product. Fail on copied code or assets (fonts, images, icons) with no licence, and on AGPL components in a proprietary service with no review. Missing licence files in the repository are an unknown with a question. A lawyer makes the actual call.

domains.title: Data model, databases and data handling
domains.summary: The schema, the migrations, the backups, and what happens at 5 million rows.

items.title: The schema was designed (keys, foreign keys, constraints, types), not improvised table by table
items.check: Review schema and migrations. Missing foreign keys, NOT NULL, unique constraints, JSON blobs holding relational data, duplicated columns across tables, stringly-typed enums.

items.title: Migrations are versioned, run forward in CI and have a rollback path
items.check: A migration tool in use (not "sync schema on boot"), down migrations or a documented expand/contract approach, and migrations run in the deploy pipeline.

items.title: Migrations avoid long table locks on large tables (concurrent index builds, batched backfills, expand then contract)
items.check: Look for ALTER TABLE adding NOT NULL with default, non-concurrent CREATE INDEX, and in-migration data backfills on big tables.

items.title: Indexes exist for real query paths (filters, joins, sorts, foreign keys)
items.check: Match WHERE/ORDER BY/JOIN columns in the code to indexes in the schema. Flag foreign keys without indexes and unbounded table scans.

items.title: N+1 queries and unbounded result sets are controlled
items.check: Loops that query per row, ORM lazy loading in list endpoints, endpoints that return every row.

items.title: Connection pooling is configured so a traffic spike cannot exhaust the database
items.check: Pool size settings, a pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, provider pooler) for serverless or multi-instance deployments, sensible timeouts.

items.title: Automated backups run at least nightly
items.check: Managed database backup settings, or backup jobs in IaC. If neither is visible in the repo, mark unknown and ask the founder to show the console setting.

items.title: A restore from backup has been performed and timed, and the steps are written down
items.check: Look for a restore runbook or drill record. Without one the status is unknown at best.

items.title: Point-in-time recovery is enabled for the database
items.check: WAL archiving or managed PITR setting with a retention window long enough to notice a bad delete.

items.title: Deletes of user-visible records are soft (recoverable) or otherwise reversible
items.check: Hard deletes in handlers for business records. Also check that every query excludes soft-deleted rows, and that unique constraints survive re-creation.

items.title: All input is validated on the server with a schema, not only in the form
items.check: A validation layer (zod, pydantic, DRF serializers, etc.) at every write entry point, with length, type and range limits.

items.title: Timestamps are stored in UTC with the user's zone kept separately, and scheduled work respects it
items.check: timestamp without time zone, local-time Date parsing, reminders computed in server local time, DST handling.

items.title: Text handling survives apostrophes, accents, emoji and right-to-left scripts in every field
items.check: UTF-8 (utf8mb4) end to end, no ASCII-only regex name validation, no length truncation by bytes, no naive SQL string building. Check PDFs and emails too.

items.title: Money is stored as integer minor units or fixed-point decimals with an explicit currency, never floats
items.check: float/double/Number columns or JS arithmetic on prices. Currency column present. Rounding rule defined in one place.

items.title: The data model can absorb a customer's "one small change" (per-tenant settings, custom fields, plan variants) without a rewrite
items.check: Hard-coded plan names and tenant-specific if-statements in code are warning signs. Is configuration data-driven?

items.title: List endpoints use pagination that stays fast and correct deep into the result set
items.check: OFFSET pagination on large tables, no max page size, no stable sort key. Cursor/keyset pagination is the fix.

items.title: Customers can export their data in a usable format without engineering help
items.check: CSV/JSON export, run as a background job for large data, tenant-scoped, protected against CSV formula injection.

items.title: Imports validate, report row-level errors and survive odd encodings, delimiters and huge files
items.check: Streaming parse, encoding detection, BOM handling, row limits, partial-failure reporting, dry-run.

items.title: Retention rules exist and code actually deletes what the contract and privacy policy say it will
items.check: Scheduled purge jobs for logs, uploads, deleted accounts and inactive data. Compare to the stated retention period in the privacy policy.

items.title: Writes that must succeed or fail together run inside a database transaction
items.check: Find flows with more than one write (create order and decrement stock, move money, create user and workspace). Fail on separate awaited writes with no transaction, a transaction opened but the writes issued on a different connection, and external calls (email, payment, AI) made inside an open transaction. Look at what the customer would see if the second write failed.

items.title: Two people or jobs updating the same record cannot silently overwrite or double-spend each other
items.check: Look for read-modify-write sequences on balances, stock, counters, seats, coupons and status fields. Passes with atomic updates (UPDATE ... SET n = n - 1 WHERE n > 0), a version column with optimistic checks, row locks (SELECT FOR UPDATE) or a unique constraint. Fail on check-then-insert with no unique index, increments computed in application memory, and "if not used then mark used" without a lock.

items.title: Foreign-key delete behaviour is chosen deliberately, so one delete cannot wipe unrelated data
items.check: Read the ON DELETE rules and ORM cascade settings. Fail on CASCADE from long-lived records (customers, workspaces, invoices) down to financial or audit records, ORM cascades that delete more than intended, and delete behaviour that was simply left at the default. Restrict or soft delete is the safer choice for anything the business must keep.

domains.title: Identity, login and sessions
domains.summary: Who is this user, can an attacker become them, and can you cut them off.

items.title: Login and signup handle plus-addressing, case, Unicode and whitespace in emails consistently
items.check: Find where emails are normalised. Same normalisation on signup, login, reset and invite? Unique index on the normalised value? Does "a+b@x.com" survive validation and email delivery?

items.title: Password reset and magic links expire, work once, and are stored hashed
items.check: Look for token expiry, single-use invalidation, hashed storage, invalidation on password change, and no token in logs or referrer-leaking URLs.

items.title: Passwords hashed with a modern slow algorithm (argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt)
items.check: Grep for md5/sha1/sha256 used on passwords, plaintext columns, home-made crypto. Provider-delegated auth (Auth0, Clerk, Supabase) is a pass.

items.title: MFA is available, and there is a recovery path for users who lose their device
items.check: TOTP/WebAuthn enrolment, recovery codes, and an identity-verified reset path that does not bypass MFA with a single email click.

items.title: Sessions time out (idle and absolute) and all sessions for one user can be revoked
items.check: Session or JWT lifetime. Stateless JWTs with no revocation list and a 30-day expiry fail this. Revocation on password change and on user disable.

items.title: Login, signup, reset and MFA endpoints are rate limited per account and per IP
items.check: Find rate-limiting middleware or provider config and confirm it covers auth routes, not just the API. In-memory limiters fail when there is more than one instance.

items.title: Lockout and throttling stop attackers without letting them lock out real users at will
items.check: Progressive delays or captcha beat hard lockout. If hard lockout exists, is there a self-service unlock, and can an attacker lock a known victim out indefinitely?

items.title: Signup, login and reset responses do not reveal whether an account exists
items.check: Compare responses and timing for known and unknown emails on reset and login.

items.title: Email is verified before it is trusted for access, invites or account linking
items.check: Social login or SSO that links to an existing account by unverified email enables account takeover. Check the linking logic.

items.title: SSO via OIDC is available for customers who require it
items.check: OIDC login per tenant, enforced-SSO setting that disables password login for that tenant, and just-in-time provisioning rules.

items.title: SAML is supported, with per-tenant configuration and signed-assertion validation
items.check: Library-based SAML (not hand-rolled XML parsing), signature validation, clock skew, certificate rotation, IdP-initiated flow decision.

items.title: SCIM provisioning deactivates a user's access the moment IT offboards them
items.check: SCIM Users/Groups endpoints, deprovisioning that also kills sessions, API keys and tokens, not just a flag nobody checks.

items.title: Access tokens are signed, verified and short-lived, and refresh tokens rotate and can be revoked
items.check: Find where JWTs or API tokens are issued and verified. Fail on verification skipped or decode-only calls, the "none" algorithm or an algorithm taken from the token header, a hard-coded or weak signing secret, access tokens that live for days, tokens kept in localStorage where XSS can read them, and refresh tokens that never rotate or cannot be revoked after logout or a password change. Provider-managed sessions (Auth0, Clerk, Supabase) are a pass if the app verifies their tokens with the provider's library and does not re-implement it.

items.title: OAuth and social login uses a state parameter, PKCE and exact redirect URIs
items.check: Look at the authorization-code flow the app implements or configures. Fail on a missing or unchecked state value (login CSRF), public clients without PKCE, wildcard or prefix-matched redirect URIs, tokens returned in URL fragments or query strings, and linking a social account to an existing account by email without a verified-email check. Not applicable if login is fully delegated and the app configures no redirect URIs of its own.

items.title: Session cookies are HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, and the session ID changes at login
items.check: Find the cookie options for the session or auth cookie. Fail on a missing HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite flag, a session ID that stays the same across login or privilege change (session fixation), session IDs in URLs, and long-lived cookies with no server-side expiry. Framework defaults count if the config does not override them.

domains.title: Infrastructure, deployment and background work
domains.summary: Getting code to production safely, keeping it up, and running work off the request path.

items.title: Dev, staging and production are separate and configured alike
items.check: Separate databases, credentials and domains per environment. Env-specific behaviour driven by config, not code branches. Production data never used in dev.

items.title: Infrastructure is defined as code, so the setup does not live in one person's memory
items.check: Terraform/Pulumi/CDK/compose/platform config files. List anything the repo implies exists but does not define.

items.title: A deploy pipeline runs tests, linting and type checks before anything reaches customers
items.check: CI workflow files. Branch protection requiring green checks cannot be seen from the repo, so ask. Deploys from a laptop are a finding.

items.title: Rollback is one click or one command and has been rehearsed
items.check: Versioned artifacts or images, platform rollback feature, and a rule for database changes that are not backwards-compatible.

items.title: Deploys are zero-downtime (health checks, rolling or blue/green, graceful shutdown, backwards-compatible schema changes)
items.check: Readiness/liveness endpoints, SIGTERM handling, deploy strategy settings.

items.title: Feature flags let you ship code without shipping the feature
items.check: A flag system and a kill switch for risky features. Flags have owners and are removed once launched.

items.title: Autoscaling or enough headroom exists for the predictable spike
items.check: Scaling policies, concurrency limits, serverless cold start and connection concerns.

items.title: Static assets are served through a CDN and cached with sensible headers
items.check: CDN config, cache-control headers, fingerprinted asset names, regional latency for target markets.

items.title: DNS, TLS certificates and domain registration auto-renew and expiries are monitored
items.check: Managed certificates or ACME renewal with alerting, registrar auto-renew, registrar account owned by the company.

items.title: Slow work (email, reports, AI calls, imports) runs on a background queue, not in the request
items.check: Long synchronous calls inside HTTP handlers, request timeouts shorter than the work, fire-and-forget promises that vanish on restart.

items.title: Outbound calls have timeouts and retries with exponential backoff and jitter
items.check: HTTP clients with no timeout, retry loops with no cap or delay, retries on non-idempotent calls.

items.title: Jobs that exhaust their retries land in a dead-letter queue that someone is alerted about
items.check: Queue config with max attempts and a DLQ, tooling to inspect and replay.

items.title: Scheduled jobs run exactly once even with multiple servers (leader election, locks or a managed scheduler)
items.check: node-cron or in-process schedulers inside the web app that will double-fire at two instances.

items.title: Caching has a stated invalidation strategy and cannot serve one user's data to another
items.check: Cache keys including tenant and user where relevant, TTLs, invalidation on writes, CDN caching of authenticated responses.

items.title: SPF, DKIM and DMARC are configured for the sending domain
items.check: Repo cannot show DNS unless IaC holds it. Ask for or suggest a dig/mail-tester check on the live domain. Transactional mail should use a separate subdomain from marketing mail.

items.title: Bounces and spam complaints are handled and suppress further sending
items.check: Email provider webhooks update a suppression list. Password reset still works for non-suppressed addresses.

items.title: Storage lifecycle rules remove temp files, old exports and stale artifacts
items.check: Bucket lifecycle policies, log retention, orphaned upload cleanup.

items.title: Cost alerts and budgets exist, including per-service caps for pay-per-use APIs, so a runaway loop is caught the same day
items.check: Cloud billing alarms, provider spend limits, and per-key caps on AI and email APIs.

items.title: A disaster recovery plan is written down and has been exercised at least once
items.check: RTO and RPO stated, steps documented, last drill dated.

items.title: A second region or failover exists if contracts promise uptime a single region cannot deliver
items.check: Compare the SLA in contracts to the architecture. Do not recommend multi-region unless a promise requires it.

items.title: Configuration is validated at boot and the app fails fast when a required setting is missing
items.check: A typed env schema. Silent fallbacks to test keys or localhost in production paths.

items.title: Databases and internal services are not reachable from the public internet
items.check: Read security groups, firewall rules, compose files, Kubernetes services and managed-database settings. Fail on 0.0.0.0/0 open to database, cache or admin ports (5432, 3306, 6379, 27017, 9200, 22), databases with public endpoints and no allow-list, and containers publishing internal ports to the host. Private subnets with only the load balancer public is the pass. Say unknown when no infrastructure code exists.

items.title: App servers keep no state locally, so any instance can be replaced or added at any time
items.check: Look for sessions, uploads, generated files, queues, rate-limit counters and caches held in process memory or on the local disk. Fail on in-memory sessions or limiters with more than one instance, user uploads written to the server filesystem, and jobs that exist only in a process array. State belongs in the database, a cache service or object storage.

items.title: Container images are small, run as a non-root user and are scanned before release
items.check: Read Dockerfiles and the CI build. Fail on no USER instruction (root at runtime), the latest tag as a base image, build tools and source left in the final image (no multi-stage build), secrets copied into layers, and no image scan step in CI. Not applicable if nothing is containerised.

items.title: Memory and CPU are bounded and monitored, and nothing in the code grows without limit
items.check: Look for container or platform memory and CPU limits and requests, and alerts on memory growth or restarts. In code, fail on module-level arrays, maps or caches that only ever grow, event listeners added per request and never removed, and whole files or result sets loaded into memory. A process that restarts every few days "because it gets slow" is the symptom.

items.title: Terraform and other infrastructure state is stored remotely, locked and encrypted, never committed
items.check: Look for a remote backend with locking and encryption. Fail on terraform.tfstate or .tfstate.backup in git (state holds secrets), a local backend on a shared project, and no locking. Not applicable if there is no infrastructure as code.

items.title: Queue and job consumers are idempotent, because the same message will sometimes arrive twice
items.check: Read the job and queue handlers. Passes with a unique key or processed-message table checked before the side effect, or operations that are naturally repeatable. Fail on handlers that send an email, charge, create a record or call a partner each time they run with no duplicate check, and on handlers that acknowledge before the work is done. "Exactly once" claims from the broker do not count as evidence.

domains.title: APIs, webhooks and third-party integrations
domains.summary: What you expose, what you consume, and what breaks when either side changes.

items.title: Inbound webhooks verify signatures, reject replays and are processed idempotently
items.check: Raw-body signature verification, timestamp tolerance, event ID dedupe table.

items.title: Outbound webhooks retry with backoff and keep a delivery log customers can inspect and replay
items.check: Delivery attempts stored, signed payloads, disabling of endpoints that fail for days, SSRF protection on customer URLs.

items.title: The public API is versioned so you can change it without breaking customer integrations
items.check: URL or header versioning, deprecation policy, changelog.

items.title: Customers can create, scope, rotate and revoke their own API keys, and keys are stored hashed
items.check: Key management UI/API, last-used timestamp, per-key scopes, prefix shown once.

items.title: API rate limits protect you without blocking legitimate integrations
items.check: Per-key and per-tenant limits, Retry-After headers, documented quotas, separate limits for expensive endpoints.

items.title: Parsing third-party responses tolerates unexpected shape changes and fails loudly, not silently
items.check: Schema validation on external responses, alerts on parse failures, pinned API versions where the vendor allows.

items.title: OAuth tokens for connected accounts refresh automatically, and refresh failure is handled and surfaced
items.check: Refresh-token flow, concurrency-safe refresh, re-authorisation prompt for users, tokens encrypted at rest.

items.title: A sandbox lets customers test their integration without touching real data
items.check: Test-mode keys and isolated data.

items.title: Every outbound third-party call has a timeout, a circuit breaker or fallback, and an owner for when the vendor is down
items.check: HTTP client defaults, failure handling in user-facing paths, graceful degradation of non-critical vendors (analytics, chat widgets).

items.title: WebSocket and server-sent event connections are authenticated, authorised per message and origin-checked
items.check: Find the socket or event-stream endpoints. Fail on connections accepted without authentication, channel or room subscriptions that trust a client-supplied ID without an ownership check, no Origin check (cross-site WebSocket hijacking), tokens in the URL that end up in logs, and no limits on connections, message size or message rate. Not applicable if the app has no real-time channels.

items.title: The API uses correct HTTP status codes and methods, so clients, caches and monitors can trust them
items.check: Fail on errors returned with status 200, GET or HEAD requests that change data (they get prefetched, cached and retried), POST used for safe reads that should be cacheable, and 500 returned for client mistakes so alerts fire on bad input. Check that retries are safe for PUT and DELETE and that creating endpoints use 201 or 409 deliberately.

domains.title: Code health and team practices
domains.summary: Whether the next human, or the next AI session, can safely change this code.

items.title: The code is readable by a human who did not write it, with consistent structure and naming
items.check: Sample several modules. Inconsistent patterns across files, god functions, magic numbers, comments that contradict code.

items.title: Every change gets a human code review before merge
items.check: Branch protection and PR history. Repos with direct pushes to main and AI-authored commits that nobody read are a finding.

items.title: A branching strategy lets two people work without overwriting each other
items.check: Branch naming, PR flow, release tagging, and a documented convention in CONTRIBUTING.

items.title: Dependencies are upgraded on a regular cadence, and nothing is two major versions behind
items.check: Compare manifests to latest releases. Automated update PRs enabled.

items.title: The framework and runtime versions still receive security patches
items.check: Node, Python, framework and database versions against vendor end-of-life dates.

items.title: Dead code, abandoned files and leftovers from the AI's earlier attempts have been deleted
items.check: Unused exports, unreferenced files, commented-out blocks, v1/v2/old/backup filenames, duplicate implementations of the same helper.

items.title: No single file has grown into an unreviewable monolith
items.check: List the largest files by line count and flag those above roughly 800 lines or with many unrelated responsibilities.

items.title: Architecture decisions are written down with their reasons
items.check: docs/adr or equivalent. Why this database, this auth approach, this tenancy model?

items.title: A README gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
items.check: Follow the README literally. Prerequisites, env vars with an example file, seed data, how to run tests. Note every step that fails or is missing.

items.title: Documentation exists for whoever inherits the system (components, data flow, third parties, how to deploy)
items.check: System diagram, list of vendors and what each is used for, deployment steps, known sharp edges.

items.title: Linting, formatting and type checking are configured and enforced
items.check: ESLint/ruff/mypy/tsc strictness, pre-commit hooks or CI enforcement, count of suppressions (any, ts-ignore, noqa).

items.title: Business rules live in one place each, not duplicated across the frontend, backend and database
items.check: Pricing, permission and validation rules re-implemented in several files with subtle differences.

items.title: Errors are handled deliberately, with no swallowed failures, unhandled rejections or half-finished operations
items.check: Grep for empty catch blocks, catch blocks that only log and continue, promises with no await or catch, missing global handlers for unhandledRejection or uncaughtException, and async handlers whose errors never reach the framework error handler. In the money and data paths, check that a failure partway through leaves the system in a consistent state and that the customer is told. Tolerate deliberate, commented ignores.

domains.title: Observability and incident response
domains.summary: Knowing it is broken before your customer does, and knowing what to do next.

items.title: Logs are structured, correlated by request ID and searchable in one place
items.check: console.log soup vs a logger with levels and JSON output, request/trace IDs, and a log destination that retains history.

items.title: Errors are captured and grouped by an error tracker, with release tagging
items.check: Sentry-style SDK in both server and client, source maps uploaded, PII scrubbing, alert rules that avoid 4,000 identical emails.

items.title: Uptime and key user journeys are checked from outside your own network
items.check: External probe on the login page and a core API route. Cannot be seen from the repo unless configured as code.

items.title: Alerts page a human, on symptoms that matter, and are tuned until they stop paging for nothing
items.check: Alert definitions with owners and thresholds, a paging tool, and a history of noisy alerts that were fixed.

items.title: Dashboards show latency, error rate and throughput for the core flows
items.check: Dashboards as code or links in the README. Metrics emitted by the app.

items.title: A single slow request can be traced across every service it touches
items.check: OpenTelemetry or vendor APM, trace IDs propagated through queues and outbound calls.

items.title: There is an on-call rotation, and a named person who picks up
items.check: Schedule in a paging tool or a documented rota with escalation. A founder who sleeps with the phone on is a bus factor of one.

items.title: Runbooks explain what each alert means and what to do first
items.check: docs/runbooks or alert annotations linking to steps.

items.title: Incidents get blameless postmortems, and the action items are tracked to done
items.check: Postmortem folder or tracker with completed follow-ups.

items.title: A status page exists so customers check it before they email you
items.check: Hosted on separate infrastructure from the app it reports on.

items.title: A written incident response plan says who leads, how customers are told and who handles a breach notification
items.check: Ask for the document. Acceptable is one page naming an incident lead, a communication channel, the status page owner, severity levels, how and when customers are told, and the legal notification deadlines that apply (for example the 72 hours in GDPR). Report unknown with a question when nothing in the repository shows it. Do not invent an answer.

domains.title: Operations, support and ownership
domains.summary: What the business needs around the code to actually run a product.

items.title: An admin panel lets your ops team do routine work without database access
items.check: Internal tooling for looking up users, plans, refunds and data fixes, protected and audit-logged.

items.title: Support tooling lets customer success answer questions without pinging engineering
items.check: Read-only account views, activity history, safe resend of emails, linking a customer-visible request ID to logs.

items.title: Customers can read a changelog of what changed and when
items.check: Public changelog or release notes, deprecation notices for API customers.

items.title: Every account, domain, repository, cloud project and vendor login belongs to the company, not to the person who built the prototype
items.check: Ask the founder to list registrar, DNS, cloud, git hosting, payment provider, app stores and email provider with the owning account for each. Personal emails as owner on any of them are a finding.

items.title: At least two people can deploy, restore a backup and rotate every credential (bus factor above one)
items.check: Who holds the root credentials and the 2FA devices? What happens if one person is unreachable for a week?

items.title: Shared credentials live in a team password manager or secrets store, not in chat, docs or someone's head
items.check: Look for credentials in README, wiki exports or setup scripts, and ask where the rest live.

domains.title: Payments and billing
domains.summary: Charging the right amount once, and being able to prove it to finance.

items.title: Charge and order creation use idempotency keys so a retry never charges twice
items.check: Idempotency-Key on provider calls, unique constraint on order/payment attempt, safe handling of timeouts after the provider has already charged.

items.title: Double-submits (four clicks on "Pay") are deduplicated on the server and disabled in the UI
items.check: Server-side dedupe on the write path, not just a disabled button.

items.title: Card numbers never touch your servers or database (hosted fields or redirect), keeping PCI scope minimal
items.check: Raw PAN/CVV in requests, logs, DB columns, or analytics events. Stripe Elements / Checkout / equivalent in use.

items.title: Provider webhooks verify signatures and are the source of truth for entitlement and payment state
items.check: Signature check with the raw body, replay window, idempotent event handling, and access granted from webhook state, not from the success-page redirect.

items.title: Currency, rounding and tax rules are defined for every country sold into
items.check: Rounding applied at a single, documented step. Zero-decimal and three-decimal currencies handled. Locale price formatting.

items.title: Sales tax and VAT are calculated, collected and reported correctly where required
items.check: A tax engine or provider tax setting (Stripe Tax, etc.), VAT ID collection for B2B, and registration in the jurisdictions where thresholds are exceeded. Needs an accountant to confirm.

items.title: Subscription upgrades, downgrades, pauses, cancellations and proration behave correctly
items.check: Plan-change code paths, proration mode, end-of-period vs immediate behaviour, entitlement changes on each transition.

items.title: Failed payments are retried on a schedule, customers are emailed (dunning), and access is handled deliberately
items.check: Smart-retry or custom schedule, dunning emails, grace period, what happens at final failure.

items.title: Refunds, credits and partial refunds work and keep revenue records consistent
items.check: Refund handlers update internal ledger, entitlement and tax. Webhook-driven refunds from the provider dashboard are handled.

items.title: Usage metering matches what is billed, to the cent, and can be audited
items.check: Events are idempotent, late events handled, billing period boundaries in UTC, and a reconciliation between raw usage and invoices.

items.title: Invoices carry required fields (legal entity, tax ID, customer PO number) and can be re-issued
items.check: Custom fields on invoices, sequential numbering, PDF generation, credit notes.

items.title: Annual and custom-term contracts can be represented without code changes
items.check: Prices, terms and discounts as data. Manual invoicing path for enterprise deals.

items.title: Finance can reconcile revenue reports against the payment provider and the bank
items.check: Exports with provider IDs, ledger of every money movement, MRR definition written down.

items.title: Chargebacks and disputes are detected, answered with evidence and tracked against revenue
items.check: Look for a handler for the provider dispute events (for example charge.dispute.created), a way to collect and submit evidence before the deadline, and entitlement and revenue handling for disputed charges. Fail on no dispute handling at all and on disputes that only surface in a provider dashboard nobody watches. The process side (who answers, within how many days) is unknown unless a document shows it.

domains.title: Application and supply-chain security
domains.summary: Secrets, dependencies, injection, uploads and the OWASP basics.

items.title: No secrets in source code, git history, client bundles, or committed .env files
items.check: Scan the working tree AND git history (run a secret scanner if available, else grep for key prefixes such as sk_, AKIA, ghp_, xox, private key blocks). Check what ships in the browser bundle (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_ variables).

items.title: Every key an AI assistant ever pasted into a config file, chat or prompt has been rotated
items.check: Cannot be verified from code. Ask the founder when keys were last rotated and whether any were shared with an AI tool. Any key that appeared in a commit, an AI chat history or a screenshot should be treated as burned.

items.title: Every installed package exists, is the one intended, and is not a look-alike (hallucinated or typosquatted names)
items.check: Review manifests and lockfiles. For each unfamiliar dependency check name spelling, publisher, age, download count and repository link. Flag packages with a handful of downloads that do something trivial.

items.title: Dependencies are scanned automatically and the lockfile is committed
items.check: Dependabot/Renovate, npm audit / pip-audit / OSV in CI, lockfile present, and install uses the lockfile (npm ci).

items.title: User input is sanitised or encoded everywhere it is rendered, preventing XSS
items.check: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, innerHTML, |safe, unescaped template output, markdown rendering without a sanitiser, user-supplied URLs in href.

items.title: Database access is parameterised; no SQL, NoSQL or command injection paths
items.check: String-built SQL, raw query helpers with interpolation, exec/system calls with user input, unsanitised filter objects passed to Mongo.

items.title: State-changing requests are protected against CSRF
items.check: CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies plus origin checks, for cookie-authenticated apps. Bearer-token-only APIs are lower risk.

items.title: SSRF, open redirects and path traversal are blocked
items.check: Server-side fetch of user-supplied URLs (webhooks, image import, link preview) without an allowlist or private-range block. Redirect targets taken from query parameters. File paths built from input.

items.title: File uploads are type-checked, size-limited, malware-scanned and stored where they cannot execute
items.check: Content sniffing not just extension, size cap, random storage names, private bucket with signed URLs, no upload inside the web root, SVG and HTML served with safe headers, virus scanning for B2B.

items.title: CORS is restricted to known origins (not "*" with credentials or reflected origin)
items.check: CORS middleware config and any manual Access-Control headers.

items.title: Security headers are set on every response (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection, referrer policy)
items.check: Middleware, framework config, or CDN/edge rules. Judge by what is configured, and suggest curl -I against the live site for confirmation.

items.title: Data is encrypted in transit everywhere and at rest in databases, buckets and backups
items.check: TLS-only connections including database and internal services, HTTP redirected, storage encryption flags in IaC or provider settings, field-level encryption for the most sensitive columns.

items.title: Everyone and everything, including AI coding agents, holds least-privilege credentials, and none holds production write access by default
items.check: IAM roles, shared root credentials, database superuser in the app connection string, production credentials in a developer's or agent's local environment. Separate read-only credentials for investigation.

items.title: Logs record who did what and never record passwords, tokens, card numbers or other sensitive fields
items.check: Logging of full request bodies, headers (Authorization, Cookie), ORM query logging with bound parameters, error reporters capturing PII. Redaction in place.

items.title: Production errors do not leak stack traces, SQL, or internals; debug mode is off
items.check: DEBUG=true defaults, verbose error handlers, GraphQL introspection and Swagger exposed in production, default admin credentials.

items.title: A penetration test has been run by someone independent, and findings fixed
items.check: Look for a report or remediation tracker. Otherwise unknown.

items.title: There are written, evidence-backed answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends
items.check: A standard answer set (SIG, CAIQ, or custom) with links to evidence: policies, screenshots, reports.

items.title: A vulnerability disclosure process exists (security.txt, a monitored security@ inbox, a response SLA)
items.check: /.well-known/security.txt, SECURITY.md, and someone who reads the inbox.

items.title: There is a documented plan for a stolen laptop or leaked credential (disk encryption, remote wipe, revocation steps)
items.check: Incident response doc, device management, list of credentials a laptop holds and how to revoke each.

items.title: Webhook endpoints, public APIs and forms are protected against automated abuse (bot protection, quotas)
items.check: Signup and contact forms with captcha or proof of work, email-sending endpoints that cannot be used as spam relays.

items.title: Secrets, tokens and signatures are compared in constant time
items.check: Grep for plain == or === comparisons on API keys, webhook signatures, reset tokens, HMACs and password-reset codes. Passes with timingSafeEqual, hmac.compare_digest, subtle.ConstantTimeCompare or the framework or provider SDK doing the check. Looking up a hashed token by an indexed value is fine.

items.title: Request body size limits and request timeouts are set, so one oversized request cannot take the app down
items.check: Look for body-parser or framework limits, reverse-proxy or platform limits, and server timeouts. Fail on unlimited JSON or text bodies, no cap on array or page-size parameters, regular expressions run on unbounded input, and handlers with no timeout at all. Upload size limits alone (SEC-09) do not count.

items.title: A threat model for the main flows exists and is revisited when features change
items.check: Ask for the document or ticket. Acceptable is one page naming what is protected, who the attackers are, and what happens if login, payments and file handling are abused. Missing is the usual state, so this is unknown with a question rather than a fail unless the repository shows the opposite.

items.title: Storage buckets are private by default and user files are served by short-lived signed URLs or an authorised endpoint
items.check: Look at bucket policies and ACLs in IaC, SDK calls that set public-read, and code that builds permanent public URLs for private user documents. Fail on public buckets that hold customer files, signed URLs that live for days or are returned to anyone without an ownership check, and guessable object keys with no authorisation in front. Public assets by design (marketing images) are fine if they live in a separate bucket. Say unknown when only the cloud console could settle it.

domains.title: Testing and quality assurance
domains.summary: Proof that the thing works, written by someone who knows what "works" means.

items.title: Business logic has unit tests that assert real expected behaviour, not just that the code runs
items.check: Sample the tests. Tests with no assertions, assertions on mocks of the thing under test, snapshot tests of everything, or tests that were clearly generated from the implementation rather than the requirement.

items.title: Tests for the money and access paths exist end to end (signup, login, checkout, permission boundaries)
items.check: Playwright/Cypress or equivalent covering the flows that make money and the flows that must refuse access.

items.title: Integration tests cover every third-party API the product depends on, against sandboxes or recorded contracts
items.check: Contract tests or a sandbox suite for payments, email, auth provider and any data API.

items.title: Every fixed bug gets a regression test
items.check: Look at recent bug-fix commits for an accompanying test.

items.title: Load testing has been done at realistic data volume before launch campaigns
items.check: k6/Locust scripts or a dated report with the production-like data size.

items.title: Test and staging data resembles production without containing production personal data
items.check: Seed scripts, anonymisation of copies. Production dumps in dev environments are a finding.

items.title: Tests run in CI on every change and a failing test blocks merge
items.check: CI config runs the suite. Skipped tests (.skip, xfail, test.todo) counted and listed.

items.title: The app has been tested on old devices, slow networks and the browsers your customers actually use
items.check: Browserslist and test matrix versus the analytics of real customers.

domains.title: Product experience
domains.summary: What the customer actually sees when things are slow, wrong, empty or in another language.

items.title: Every screen has designed empty, loading and error states
items.check: Data-fetching components with no loading or error branch, blank screens on empty lists, infinite spinners.

items.title: Error messages tell the customer what happened and what to do next, instead of "something went wrong"
items.check: Generic catch-all messages, raw exception text in the UI, errors with no recovery action or support reference ID.

items.title: Forms keep what people typed when one field fails validation, and show errors next to the field
items.check: Controlled state vs full page reload, server errors mapped to fields.

items.title: Pages and bundles are light enough for hotel wifi and mid-range phones
items.check: Bundle size, image optimisation, blocking requests, no waterfall of sequential fetches, offline/slow-network behaviour on critical flows.

items.title: Transactional emails render correctly in the mail clients your customers use
items.check: Table-based or tested templating (MJML/React Email), plain-text alternatives, dark mode, test across clients.

items.title: Notifications can be turned off per channel and category, and marketing email has a working unsubscribe
items.check: Preference centre, List-Unsubscribe headers, enforcement on send, legal-required footer details.

items.title: Destructive actions have confirmation or undo
items.check: Delete buttons that act immediately, bulk operations with no preview.

items.title: The app is usable by keyboard and screen reader (semantic HTML, labels, focus management, contrast)
items.check: Clickable divs, unlabeled inputs, modal focus traps, missing alt text, colour-only meaning.

items.title: Text is translatable, and dates, numbers and currencies are formatted per locale
items.check: Hard-coded strings, concatenated sentences, Intl usage, plural rules, text expansion and RTL layout.

items.title: The back button, deep links, refresh and multiple tabs behave as people expect
items.check: State kept in URL for filters and steps, no history trapping, safe re-submit after refresh.
